passage:
Dear Ujjwal,

You asked how the first month abroad is going, and I have a small funny story. In the lab corridor I wanted to call my lab partner over, so I did what we do at home: palm down, fingers scooping the air towards me. Nothing. He frowned, then came slowly with a puzzled look. Yesterday I saw a local student beckon someone with an upturned finger, and the person laughed and came straight over. Then in the canteen queue a staff member glanced at that same finger with a stiff face. So it isn't the same everywhere, even here.

I've decided to stop guessing. I use words now, "could you come?", and I watch what people do.

Miss you all. 🙂

Parveen

qa.q: What gesture did Parveen use to call the lab partner?
qa.a: Parveen used a palm-down scoop of the fingers towards the body.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling about the beckoning puzzle?
qa.a: Parveen was amused but a little unsure, since the gesture got a frown from one person and a laugh from another. Deciding to use words and watch others suggests Parveen wants to avoid causing offence.

qa.q: What could a student new to a country do about unfamiliar gestures?
qa.a: Use plain words to call people, watch what locals do, and ask a friendly classmate what a gesture means.

qa.q: How might the lab partner have seen the palm-down scoop?
qa.a: The lab partner frowned and came slowly with a puzzled look, so the scoop may have seemed unclear or odd rather than friendly.

grounding: A student abroad finds beckoning gestures mean different things and chooses to watch locals and use words.

passage: Imran, it's Usha, remember when I told you about my first term in Norway? The funniest part was the beckoning. In my first week I called a course-mate over with the palm-down scoop we use back home, and she just laughed and said it looked like I was sweeping crumbs. Another time I crooked one finger upwards at a boy at the bus stop, thinking it was very casual, and he raised his eyebrows and stepped back. I felt my ears go hot. My housemate said in some places that finger is rude, or at least bossy. So I started asking, "Is it okay if I call you like this?", and I copied the way the locals waved. Guessing from home habits was the mistake.

qa.q: Where was Usha's first term?
qa.a: Usha's first term was in Norway.

qa.q: How did Usha feel when the boy raised his eyebrows and stepped back?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed, shown by the ears going hot, and realised the crooked finger had landed badly. The boy's reaction may also have been plain surprise, so it is a cue rather than proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Usha to do in a new country when calling someone?
qa.a: Ask politely, use a word or a wave that locals use, and avoid assuming home gestures will carry the same meaning.

qa.q: What was it like for the course-mate when Usha used the scoop?
qa.a: The course-mate found it funny, and said it looked like sweeping crumbs, so the meaning simply didn't carry over.

grounding: A student abroad learns that a beckon friendly in one place is rude or odd in another, and that asking and watching is wiser.

passage: I'm Jyoti, and I was sitting opposite Vishal in our university canteen in Manila, three weeks into the exchange. He wanted more water, so he lifted his hand, palm up, and curled one finger at the server. She came, but her face had gone flat, and she set the jug down harder than needed. Vishal didn't seem to notice, or maybe he did; he rubbed the back of his neck afterwards. Our classmate Marites leaned over and said quietly that many people here use that sign only for dogs. Vishal went red. Marites showed us how she calls someone: palm down, fingers scooping towards herself, exactly like my grandmother does back home. The next day I saw Vishal raise his hand, palm down, scoop gently and smile at the same server. She smiled back.

qa.q: How did Marites show she calls someone?
qa.a: Palm down, fingers scooping towards herself.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when Marites explained the sign?
qa.a: He went red, which suggests he felt embarrassed; rubbing his neck earlier may mean he already sensed something was off, or it may have been nothing.

qa.q: What did Vishal do well the next day?
qa.a: He used the palm-down scoop Marites showed and added a smile, which showed respect for how people there call someone.

qa.q: How did the server seem to see Vishal's finger beckon?
qa.a: Her flat face and the jug set down hard suggest she felt treated rudely, as if called like a dog.

grounding: Shows a student abroad learning that the upturned-finger beckon is rude there and that the palm-down scoop is the local way.

passage:
Day one. In the university library in Melbourne, Seema spotted Emma from her tutorial group and called her over the way she would at home: palm down, fingers scooping. Emma gave a small awkward smile and walked the other way. Seema sat very still, wondering what she had done.
Day three. Over chai in the hostel kitchen, Seema told Karthik, who had studied there for three years. He laughed gently. "Here that can look like 'go away'. Most people wave with the palm up or just say your name." Then he added, "Or maybe she was late for class. Don't decide yet."
Day six. Seema saw Emma across the quad, waved high and called, "Emma, over here!" Emma jogged across. When Seema explained, Emma groaned. "I thought you were shooing me off! I felt so rude walking away."

qa.q: What did Karthik say most people there do instead of the scoop?
qa.a: Most people wave with the palm up or just say your name.

qa.q: How was Seema feeling after Emma walked away on day one?
qa.a: She was confused and a little hurt, sitting very still and wondering what she had done; she could not yet tell whether Emma was offended or just busy.

qa.q: What made Karthik's advice wise?
qa.a: He explained the local meaning but also warned Seema not to decide yet, which kept her from assuming Emma disliked her.

qa.q: What was it like for Emma when Seema made the palm-down gesture?
qa.a: Emma thought she was being shooed away, felt awkward, and later felt bad about walking off.

grounding: Shows a student abroad finding that a palm-down beckon friendly at home can read as 'go away' elsewhere, and learning by asking.

passage: Bhavna beti, you leave for your course next month, so let your old Rafiq Chacha tell you about my first ship. I was twenty-one, a trainee engineer, and the captain was a tall Norwegian named Mr Hagen. One morning in the engine room I needed him to look at a leaking valve. I called him the way my mother called me at home: hand out, palm down, fingers scooping. He looked at me, nodded, and walked away up the ladder. I stood there fuming, thinking he did not care about my valve. At lunch the cook, who had sailed with many crews, told me that for the captain my scoop looked like 'go on, off you go'. So that evening I went up, said his name clearly and asked him to come. He came at once. After that, in every new port, I watched how the dockworkers called each other before I ever lifted a hand.

qa.q: What did young Rafiq need the captain to look at?
qa.a: He needed him to look at a leaking valve.

qa.q: How did young Rafiq feel when the captain walked away up the ladder?
qa.a: He was angry, standing there fuming, because he thought the captain did not care about the valve; in fact it was a misreading of his gesture.

qa.q: What choice in the story fixed the problem with the captain?
qa.a: Rafiq went up, said the captain's name clearly and asked him to come, using words instead of a gesture that meant something else to him.

qa.q: How did Mr Hagen likely see Rafiq's palm-down scoop?
qa.a: He probably read it as being sent off, so he nodded and left, not realising Rafiq was calling him closer.

grounding: Shows a young trainee learning that a palm-down beckon can read as 'go away' to someone from another culture, and that watching locals and asking works better.

passage: Typhoon rain drummed so hard on the tin roof of the Manila university canteen that nobody could hear anyone calling. Gurpreet had been studying there for three weeks. Across the room his classmate Anand hooked one finger upward at the server, the way people do in films, to call her over. The server's face tightened, and she took her time coming. Gurpreet noticed something else: a local student at the next table, soaked through, held her hand out palm-down and made a small scooping motion, the same gesture his Nani used back in Ludhiana. The server came at once, smiling. Later, dripping under the bus shelter, Gurpreet asked his lab partner Marisol about it. "The curled finger? We use that for dogs," she said, wincing. "Most people won't say anything, but it stings." Anand went quiet. "I had no idea," he said. "I'll watch people here more before I use my hands."

qa.q: What gesture did the local student use to call the server?
qa.a: She held her hand out palm-down and made a small scooping motion.

qa.q: How did Anand likely feel after Marisol's explanation?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and a little guilty, since he had meant the curled finger as an ordinary call and had not known it could sting.

qa.q: What lesson does Gurpreet's watching show?
qa.a: Watching how local people signal, and asking someone like Marisol, is wiser than assuming a gesture means the same as at home.

qa.q: What was it like for the server when Anand curled his finger at her?
qa.a: She likely felt disrespected, as if being called like a dog, which is why her face tightened and she took her time.

grounding: It illustrates students abroad learning that the upturned-finger beckon can be rude where the palm-down scoop is normal, and that watching locals and asking is wiser than guessing.
